name: Daba
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Lienhard, Ruth & M. Giger. 1986 (révisé en 2009). Document de référence pour la standardisation de la langue daba. Yaoundé: Société Internationale de Linguistique (SIL Cameroun). 28 pp. (copy consulted: Internet Archive 2010-11-28 capture of the silcam.org download).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonologie, §2.5 Les tons: §2.5.1 Les tonèmes, p. 14; §2.5.2 Les schèmes tonals, pp. 14-15; §2.5.3 Fonction du ton, p. 15
catalog_quote: Dans la langue daba chaque syllabe est charactérisée par un ton propre. Trois régistres tonals sont observés: haut (marqué par un accent ́), moyen (non marqué dans les formes orthographiques, mais avec an accent ̄ dans les formes phonétiques) et bas (marqué par un accent ̀). En plus nous avons relevé un ton modulé bas (marqué par un accent ̂) sur certains pronoms sujet. ... Il est à remarquer qu’il y a des restrictions dans la distribution des schèmes tonals pour les verbes et les noms. Les verbes monosyllabiques manifestent seulement un ton bas ou bien un ton moyen. Le ton initial des verbes dissyllabiques est toujours bas. Il n’y a pas de verbes trisyllabiques. Le premier ton des noms dissyllabiques et trisyllabiques est toujours bas ou moyen, mais les adverbes, les adjectives ainsi que les idéophones ont souvent un ton initial haut. ... L’opposition entre les tons a très peu de distribution sur le plan lexical. ... Sur le plan grammatical le ton sert à marquer le focus selectif dans le sujet (ton haut), ainsi que l’emphase du verbe (ton haut). Le perfectif et l’imperfectif sont aussi marqués par le ton (bas pour le perfectif, haussé pour l’imperfectif).

new_statements.translation: In the Daba language every syllable is characterised by its own tone. Three tonal registers are observed: high (marked with an acute accent), mid (unmarked in orthographic forms, but with a macron in phonetic forms) and low (marked with a grave accent). In addition we have noted a low modulated (falling) tone (marked with a circumflex) on certain subject pronouns. [...] The opposition between tones has very little distribution on the lexical level.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Daba is a register-tone language: every syllable bears one of three level tones (H, M, L), plus a low falling tone on some subject pronouns; tone melodies are restricted by word class (monosyllabic verbs only L or M; first tone of disyllabic verbs always L; first tone of di-/trisyllabic nouns L or M; adverbs, adjectives and ideophones often H-initial). Tone is marginally lexical but marks grammatical categories (subject focus, verb emphasis, perfective/imperfective, directional, clause relations). The source says nothing about word stress or accent d'intensité.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress discussed at all).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone-pattern restrictions by word class (verbs vs nouns vs adverbs/adjectives/ideophones); one unresolved case, the pronoun ta, whose meanings differ by tone and vowel length (§2.5.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Description is at the level of the phonological word (mots monosyllabiques/dissyllabiques/trisyllabiques) with phrase-level grammatical tone also described; based on the Pologozom variety used as the standard.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes the Pologozom variety (Daba proper), which SIL used as the reference dialect for the Daba standard; Glottolog lists Nive and Pologozom as dialects of nucl1683. It explicitly distinguishes Daba-propre from Daba-Mazagway (maza1304) and Daba-Kola (separate languoid); the tone statement applies to Daba proper/Pologozom.

Three tone registers are observed: high (marked by an acute accent), mid (unmarked in orthographic forms, but with a macron in phonetic forms) and low (marked by a grave accent). new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Daba (world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule field and the existing statement, taken from this same work at the same locator, reads 'tone language, no stress statement'. Re-reading the whole document confirms that reading verbatim: §2.5.1 and §2.5.3 are the deciding passages and nowhere does the work state a stress placement or deny stress. No new placement claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Daba is described as a register tone language: every syllable bears one of three level tones (H, M, L), plus a low falling tone on some subject pronouns; all 4 patterns occur on monosyllables, all 9 on disyllables, 15 of 27 on trisyllables. Tone has little lexical yield and works mainly grammatically (subject focus, verb emphasis, perfective/imperfective, directional, clause linkage). The document contains no statement about word stress, accent d'intensité or prominence; the only 'accent' tokens name the tone diacritics, and 'prosodie' (§2.3.3) refers to palatalisation/labialisation prosodies spreading over the phonological word, not to stress. Vowel length is mentioned only for the pronoun ta (§2.5.4) and for reduced non-final syllable nuclei (§2.1.3).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (no stress discussion at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Tone-pattern restrictions by word class (§2.5.2, p. 15): monosyllabic verbs carry only L or M; the initial tone of disyllabic verbs is always L; there are no trisyllabic verbs; the first tone of di- and trisyllabic nouns is always L or M, whereas adverbs, adjectives and ideophones often have an initial H tone. Nothing on stress exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: The work states (§1.2, printed p. 2 / p. 3) that the description concerns 'seulement le daba propre', i.e. Daba proper — the plain dialect (Douroum, Pologozom, Kombom, Mandama; the authors' own 1975 fieldwork was on the Pologozom parler) and the mountain dialect (Matalao, Nivé, Tima, Nduzen) — and explicitly not Daba-Mazagway (Mouchet 1966, Wedekind 1976) or Daba-Kola, which it treats as sister dialects of one language. This matches Glottolog nucl1683 'Daba'; Mazagway is catalogued separately (maza1304).
